endorsements.quote: The human clinician must retain ultimate authority, accountability, and responsibility for all clinical decisions ( 20 ).

The interface must be designed with user-centered principles to seamlessly integrate into clinical workflows, ensuring that verifying AI outputs does not become a burden that detracts from patient care.
Clinicians must be retrained to verify rather than blindly trust these algorithmic recommendations.
Crucially, this training must cultivate a mindset of healthy skepticism and critical appraisal.
Medical, psychology, and nursing curricula must include foundational training on the principles, capabilities, and limitations of AI in clinical contexts ( 23 ).

unlisted_practices: Mandate explicit disclosure of AI use in consent forms and obtain patients' full informed consent for AI use in mental health care.
Require fairness audits on AI tools used in mental healthcare.
Use explainable AI to identify biased reasoning in AI tools.
Legislate a human-in-the-loop requirement for all high-risk clinical decisions.
Prohibit AI use for autonomous crisis response and route AI alerts to a human professional.
Enforce strict compliance with data protection laws such as HIPAA for mental health data.
Use privacy-preserving techniques and mandate clear data use policies for sensitive mental health data.
Establish rigorous validation standards for AI medical devices through regulators such as FDA or MHRA.
Require explainability of AI tools as a prerequisite for safe deployment so clinicians can scrutinize AI reasoning.
Adopt a risk-based governance framework grounded in international ethical principles such as WHO's.
Prioritize research on human-AI collaboration and co-designing equitable tools with underserved communities.

screen.reason: This is a perspective article presenting the 'Augmented Clinician' framework for human-AI collaboration in mental healthcare.
